planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; a dense mulch layer helps conserve moisture while the shallow root system establishes.

directions: Everlow is a compact, low-mounding hybrid yew that stays under knee height while spreading several feet wide, forming an exceptionally dense, flat-topped carpet of fine dark green needles. It is among the most reliably shade-tolerant of all groundcover conifers, thriving under high tree canopy or on the north side of buildings where few other evergreens perform, though it also accepts considerable sun in cooler climates. Grow in moist, well-drained soil and avoid low spots that stay wet, which invites root rot. As with all yews, foliage and seeds are toxic if ingested, so site thoughtfully around pets and small children.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; its extremely narrow habit makes it well suited to tight side yards, foundation gaps, and vertical accent plantings in deep shade.

directions: Beanpole is a strikingly narrow, strictly columnar English yew that grows slowly upward while staying only a foot or two wide for decades, making it one of the few evergreens that can furnish year-round screening or a vertical accent in a space too tight for almost any other conifer. It tolerates deep shade as well as the species, holding dense, dark green needle coverage from top to bottom even against a shaded wall or fence line. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and avoid waterlogged ground. All parts except the fleshy red aril are toxic if eaten, so place it away from areas where pets or children forage.

common_name: Semperaurea Golden Yew (Golden Upright English Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; some open sky or dappled light helps the gold color hold best, though the plant tolerates considerably more shade than most golden conifers.

directions: Semperaurea is one of the oldest and most dependable golden-foliage yews, a slow-growing male clone (so it sets no berries) with an upright-spreading habit and consistently deep gold-yellow needles that hold their color through winter better than most other golden conifers, which often fade or bronze. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, where it retains both density and color far better than true full-shade sites; it still tolerates more shade than virtually any other golden-foliage evergreen. Established plants need only occasional light shaping to maintain their naturally dense, rounded-upright form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; dappled morning light brings out the brightest gold margins on new growth.

directions: Summergold is a low, wide-spreading Dutch yew cultivar whose new spring growth emerges bright creamy-gold before settling to green needles edged in gold, giving a two-toned groundcover effect through the growing season. It stays well under two feet tall while slowly spreading into a dense mat, making it useful as a durable evergreen groundcover beneath high canopy or along shaded foundation beds. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade for the best variegation; deeper shade is tolerated but muted color follows. As with all yews, foliage and seed are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; protect from drying winter wind, which can brown the tightly twisted foliage.

directions: Spiralis is an old Japanese selection of Hinoki cypress whose sprays of scale-like foliage twist and curl along the branches in a distinctive spiraled pattern, giving a sculptural, almost hand-carved texture unlike any straight-foliaged conifer. It grows slowly into a loose, upright pyramidal form and performs well in the dappled light of a woodland garden, where strong hot sun can bronze the fine foliage in summer. Grow in consistently moist but well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and shelter from harsh winter wind to prevent tip burn. Its unusual texture makes it a strong specimen or accent plant for shaded Japanese-style or collector conifer gardens.

common_name: Pygmaea Argentea Lawson Cypress (Dwarf Silver-Tipped Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; this cultivar resents hot, dry exposure far more than most Lawson cypress forms.

directions: Pygmaea Argentea is a Victorian-era Lawson cypress selection, grown since the late 1800s, that forms a dense, slow-growing dwarf globe to broad pyramid of blue-green foliage, with new spring growth emerging creamy silver-white at the branch tips before aging to blue-green. The contrast between fresh silvered growth and older foliage gives the plant a frosted appearance for several weeks each year. Grow in cool, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, where it is far less prone to the summer heat stress and foliage browning that afflicts this cultivar in full, hot sun. Its compact size and refined texture suit rock gardens, trough plantings, and shaded dwarf-conifer collections.

common_name: Golden Sprite Hinoki Cypress (Miniature Gold Mounding Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade, in a trough, raised bed, or rock garden where its tiny scale can be appreciated up close.

directions: Golden Sprite is an extremely slow-growing miniature Hinoki cypress that forms a tight, irregular gold-yellow mound rarely reaching much over a foot tall even after many years, making it a favorite among dwarf conifer collectors for troughs and rock gardens. Its color holds reasonably well in partial shade, which also helps prevent the foliage scorch that bright, hot, full sun can cause on many golden conifer cultivars. Grow in moist but sharply drained soil, since this miniature form is more sensitive to soggy roots than larger Hinoki cypress cultivars. Its diminutive size and bright color make it a focal accent rather than a mass planting.

common_name: Yewtopia Plum Yew (Compact Spreading Patented Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade; space to allow for its wide, flat-spreading habit.

directions: Yewtopia (US Plant Patent 7,168,137, cultivar 'Plania') is a compact, flat-spreading Southern Living Plant Collection selection of Japanese plum yew that stays a dense 3 to 4 feet tall and wide, usable as a low hedge, foundation planting, or broad groundcover-style mass. Like the species, it tolerates deep shade, root competition from established trees, heat, and humidity far better than true Taxus yews, and unlike Taxus it is largely left alone by deer, making it a dependable shade-garden alternative to pachysandra or liriope at a larger scale. Grow in well-drained, average to fertile soil; it is slow-growing and needs little pruning to maintain its naturally dense, spreading form. A good low-maintenance choice for filling deep-shade beds where turf and most groundcovers fail.
sources: North Carolina State Extension -- Plants Database
